# LLM-Based User Profile System: Design Document

---

## Section 1: Full Profile Schema

### Design Philosophy

Each layer is a **derived artifact** — never raw data. The layers form a pyramid: L1 is the most stable and most expensive to update; L5 is ephemeral and cheap. Higher layers inform prompt context when generating lower layers (e.g., L1 occupation informs how L3 interests are interpreted).

---

### L1 — Identity (Monthly)

```json
{
  "layer": "L1",
  "version": 7,
  "generated_at": "2024-11-01T00:00:00Z",
  "next_refresh": "2024-12-01T00:00:00Z",

  "occupation": {
    "inferred_role": "Senior Software Engineer",
    "confidence": 0.87,
    "domain": "backend_infrastructure",
    "evidence_summary": "Frequent visits to AWS docs, GitHub, system design content"
  },

  "expertise_domains": [
    { "domain": "distributed_systems", "level": "expert",     "confidence": 0.91 },
    { "domain": "python",             "level": "proficient",  "confidence": 0.85 },
    { "domain": "machine_learning",   "level": "intermediate","confidence": 0.62 }
  ],

  "communication_style": {
    "preferred_register":   "technical",
    "verbosity_preference": "concise",
    "analogy_receptivity":  "low",
    "jargon_tolerance":     "high",
    "evidence_style":       "data_driven"
  },

  "inferred_timezone": "America/Los_Angeles",
  "inferred_language": "en-US",
  "secondary_languages": ["es"],

  "schema_version": "1.2"
}
```

**Relation to other layers:** L1 is consumed as *system context* by every downstream summarization prompt. The `expertise_domains` field prevents L3 from re-flagging well-known topics as "new interests" — e.g., a Python expert visiting a Python tutorial is not developing a new interest.

---

### L2 — Preferences (Weekly)

```json
{
  "layer": "L2",
  "version": 14,
  "generated_at": "2024-11-18T00:00:00Z",
  "next_refresh": "2024-11-25T00:00:00Z",

  "content_preferences": {
    "preferred_length":     "medium",
    "preferred_format":     ["bullet_lists", "code_blocks", "tables"],
    "disliked_format":      ["long_prose", "heavy_metaphor"],
    "source_preferences":   ["official_docs", "technical_blogs", "arxiv"],
    "paywall_tolerance":    "low"
  },

  "topical_filters": {
    "topics_to_avoid":      ["celebrity_news", "sports", "cryptocurrency"],
    "sensitive_topics":     ["politics"],
    "confidence_in_avoids": 0.78
  },

  "interaction_preferences": {
    "prefers_proactive_suggestions": false,
    "preferred_response_tone":       "direct",
    "follow_up_questions_tolerance": "low",
    "citation_preference":           "always_cite"
  },

  "temporal_patterns": {
    "peak_work_hours":   "09:00-18:00 PT",
    "weekend_behavior":  "lighter_browsing",
    "context_switch_frequency": "high"
  },

  "schema_version": "1.2"
}
```

**Relation to other layers:** L2 governs *how* responses are delivered. L3/L4 govern *what* content is relevant. An AI assistant combines both: "discuss this topic (L3), but format it as bullet points with citations (L2)."

---

### L3 — Interests (Daily)

```json
{
  "layer": "L3",
  "version": 31,
  "generated_at": "2024-11-19T06:00:00Z",
  "next_refresh": "2024-11-20T06:00:00Z",

  "interest_clusters": [
    {
      "cluster_id":   "cl_001",
      "label":        "LLM Infrastructure & Serving",
      "confidence":   0.94,
      "velocity":     "rising",
      "first_seen":   "2024-09-12",
      "last_active":  "2024-11-18",
      "signal_count": 47,
      "subtopics":    ["vLLM", "KV cache optimization", "inference batching"],
      "decay_rate":   "slow"
    },
    {
      "cluster_id":   "cl_002",
      "label":        "Rust Systems Programming",
      "confidence":   0.71,
      "velocity":     "stable",
      "first_seen":   "2024-10-01",
      "last_active":  "2024-11-15",
      "signal_count": 19,
      "subtopics":    ["memory safety", "async runtime", "tokio"],
      "decay_rate":   "medium"
    },
    {
      "cluster_id":   "cl_003",
      "label":        "Home Renovation",
      "confidence":   0.55,
      "velocity":     "falling",
      "first_seen":   "2024-10-20",
      "last_active":  "2024-11-01",
      "signal_count": 8,
      "subtopics":    ["kitchen remodel", "contractor pricing"],
      "decay_rate":   "fast"
    }
  ],

  "dormant_interests": [
    { "label": "Kubernetes", "last_active": "2024-08-30", "archived_confidence": 0.81 }
  ],

  "schema_version": "1.2"
}
```

**Relation to other layers:** L3 clusters directly seed L4 — the LLM checks if recent activity (L4) aligns with, diverges from, or creates new entries in L3. L5 cards are always subordinate to an L3 cluster or create a provisional one.

---

### L4 — World Context (Daily)

```json
{
  "layer": "L4",
  "version": 31,
  "generated_at": "2024-11-19T06:00:00Z",
  "next_refresh": "2024-11-20T06:00:00Z",

  "active_projects": [
    {
      "project_id":    "proj_001",
      "label":         "Migrate inference service to vLLM",
      "inferred_from": "repeated visits to vLLM GitHub, Stack Overflow q about CUDA OOM errors",
      "status":        "in_progress",
      "confidence":    0.83,
      "started":       "2024-11-10",
      "last_active":   "2024-11-18"
    }
  ],

  "recent_search_themes": [
    { "theme": "vLLM PagedAttention internals", "query_count": 6,  "last_queried": "2024-11-18" },
    { "theme": "Rust tokio select macro",       "query_count": 3,  "last_queried": "2024-11-17" }
  ],

  "current_news_topics": [
    { "topic": "OpenAI o3 release",       "engagement": "high",   "sentiment": "curious"  },
    { "topic": "EU AI Act enforcement",   "engagement": "medium", "sentiment": "neutral"  }
  ],

  "open_context_threads": [
    {
      "thread_id":  "ctx_001",
      "summary":    "Comparing vLLM vs TensorRT-LLM for internal deployment",
      "confidence": 0.76,
      "expires":    "2024-11-26T06:00:00Z"
    }
  ],

  "schema_version": "1.2"
}
```

**Relation to other layers:** L4 is the most actionable layer for the AI assistant at request time — it tells the assistant *what the user is doing right now*, so it can proactively offer relevant help. L4 is heavily informed by L3 clusters (only signals that map to a known cluster or exceed a novelty threshold are included).

---

### L5 — Interest Cards (Event-Triggered, 48h TTL)

```json
{
  "layer": "L5",
  "cards": [
    {
      "card_id":        "card_abc123",
      "trigger_pattern":"deep_dive_single_topic",
      "topic":          "Flash Attention 3 paper",
      "summary":        "User read the FA3 arXiv paper, highlighted 3 sections on I/O complexity, copied code snippet from implementation section",
      "parent_cluster": "cl_001",
      "signals_used": [
        { "type": "page_visit",  "url_domain": "arxiv.org",  "duration_sec": 840, "scroll_depth": 0.95 },
        { "type": "highlight",   "content_hash": "h_7f3a",   "context": "I/O complexity paragraph" },
        { "type": "copy_event",  "content_hash": "h_2b9c",   "context": "CUDA kernel snippet" }
      ],
      "ai_hint":        "User is actively studying Flash Attention 3 implementation details; assume deep technical familiarity",
      "created_at":     "2024-11-19T14:23:00Z",
      "expires_at":     "2024-11-21T14:23:00Z",
      "eviction_policy":"ttl_or_superseded"
    }
  ],

  "schema_version": "1.2"
}
```

---

## Section 2: Generation Pipeline

### L1 — Identity Pipeline

| Attribute | Detail |
|-----------|--------|
| **Input** | 30-day aggregated signal batch: top domains visited, query vocabulary, content types consumed, copy/highlight patterns |
| **Trigger** | Monthly cron + manual trigger if `signal_count_since_last_run > 5000` |
| **Merge Strategy** | **Weighted merge**: new generation gets 0.6 weight, existing L1 gets 0.4 weight for numeric confidence scores. Categorical fields (role, style) overwrite only if new confidence > existing confidence + 0.1 (hysteresis to prevent thrash) |

**Summarization Prompt:**
```
SYSTEM: You are a user modeling assistant. You infer stable professional and 
communicative attributes from browser behavior. Never infer sensitive categories 
(health, religion, politics, ethnicity). Output valid JSON matching the schema provided.

USER:
You are updating the Identity profile (L1) for a user.

EXISTING L1 PROFILE:
{{existing_l1_json}}

BEHAVIORAL SUMMARY (last 30 days):
- Top 20 domains by visit time: {{domain_list}}
- Top 50 search query stems: {{query_stems}}
- Content interaction patterns: {{interaction_summary}}
- Vocabulary complexity score: {{vocab_score}}
- Average session technical depth score: {{tech_depth}}

CURRENT DATE: {{date}}

TASK: Generate an updated L1 profile. For each field, provide a confidence score 
(0.0–1.0) and a one-line evidence_summary. Do not include PII. Do not infer 
health, religion, political, or ethnic attributes. If evidence is insufficient 
for a field, retain the existing value unchanged.

OUTPUT FORMAT: Return only valid JSON matching this schema: {{l1_schema}}
```

---

### L2 — Preferences Pipeline

| Attribute | Detail |
|-----------|--------|
| **Input** | 7-day signal batch: content format of highly-engaged pages (scroll depth > 0.7, dwell > 120s), explicit saves/bookmarks, topic filter signals (rapid back-navigation = implicit dislike) |
| **Trigger** | Weekly cron (Monday 3am local inferred timezone) |
| **Merge Strategy** | **Append + deduplicate for lists** (topics_to_avoid), **overwrite with recency bias** for scalar preferences. Existing preferences survive unless contradicted by ≥3 signals |

**Summarization Prompt:**
```
SYSTEM: You are a preference modeling assistant. Infer content and interaction 
preferences from engagement signals. Be conservative — only assert a preference 
if supported by multiple consistent signals. Output valid JSON.

USER:
EXISTING L2 PROFILE: {{existing_l2_json}}
L1 CONTEXT: {{l1_occupation}}, {{l1_style}}

ENGAGEMENT SIGNALS (last 7 days):
- High-engagement content samples (title, format, length): {{high_engage_samples}}
- Low-engagement bounce patterns (rapid exits): {{bounce_samples}}
- Explicit saves: {{bookmark_titles}}
- Search refinement patterns: {{refinement_patterns}}

TASK: Update the L2 preferences profile. Flag any preference that appears in 
conflict with existing preferences — do not silently overwrite. Output the 
full updated profile plus a "conflicts_detected" array.
```

---

### L3 — Interests Pipeline

| Attribute | Detail |
|-----------|--------|
| **Input** | 24-hour signal batch (URLs, titles, domains, dwell times, searches, highlights), plus current L3 to allow delta updates |
| **Trigger** | Daily cron at 6am local time. Also triggered if a burst of >20 signals on a single topic arrives within 2 hours (real-time path) |
| **Merge Strategy** | **Cluster-level merge**: existing clusters get their `signal_count` and `confidence` updated; new clusters are appended; clusters with zero signals for 7 days get `velocity: falling`; after 21 days inactive they move to `dormant_interests` |

**Full Example Prompt (shown in Section 4)**

---

### L4 — World Context Pipeline

| Attribute | Detail |
|-----------|--------|
| **Input** | 24-48 hour signal batch, current L3 clusters, previous L4 |
| **Trigger** | Daily at 6am + event-triggered if `active_project` signals surge (≥10 signals same domain cluster within 4 hours) |
| **Merge Strategy** | **Differential update**: projects are updated in place (status, last_active); threads expire on schedule; new themes append with deduplication; stale themes (>72h no signal) are pruned |

**Summarization Prompt:**
```
SYSTEM: You are a context modeling assistant. Identify what the user is actively 
working on or investigating right now, based on recent browser signals.

USER:
CURRENT L3 INTERESTS: {{l3_clusters_summary}}
EXISTING L4: {{existing_l4_json}}

SIGNALS (last 24-48 hours):
{{signal_batch}}

TASK:
1. Identify active projects (multi-session, goal-oriented behavior on a coherent topic)
2. Summarize recent search themes (without storing raw queries)
3. Note any news topics the user engaged with deeply
4. Identify open context threads (comparisons, decisions in progress)

For each item, note confidence (0–1) and which L3 cluster it maps to (or "novel").
Prune items from existing L4 not evidenced in the last 48h.
Output valid JSON matching: {{l4_schema}}
```

---

### L5 — Interest Cards Pipeline

#### Trigger Pattern 1: Deep Dive Single Topic
**Condition:** `dwell_time > 600s AND scroll_depth > 0.85 AND (highlight_count >= 2 OR copy_event_count >= 1)` on a single page or domain cluster within a 30-minute window.

**Rationale:** The user is doing serious, focused reading — not casual browsing. This card should prime the AI assistant to assume deep familiarity with that specific content.

#### Trigger Pattern 2: Repeated Cross-Session Search Refinement
**Condition:** `≥4 searches with overlapping query stems within 24h, across ≥2 browsing sessions, with click-throughs on ≥3 different result domains`.

**Rationale:** The user hasn't found a satisfying answer yet — they're stuck or researching actively. The card should signal "user is in research mode on this topic, proactive suggestions would be welcome."

#### Trigger Pattern 3: Comparative Research Pattern
**Condition:** `≥3 page visits to pages whose titles/domains match a comparison pattern (e.g., "X vs Y", side-by-side visits to competitor/alternative sites) within a 4-hour window`.

**Example:** Visiting `vllm.ai`, `tensorrt-llm docs`, `triton inference server docs` in sequence, or searching "vllm vs tensorrt benchmark".

**Rationale:** The user is making a decision. The card should signal this so the AI assistant can offer comparison-oriented help proactively.

#### Card Schema
```json
{
  "card_id":         "string (uuid)",
  "trigger_pattern": "enum: deep_dive | research_stuck | comparative_research",
  "topic":           "string: LLM-inferred topic label",
  "summary":         "string: 1-2 sentence description of what user is doing",
  "parent_cluster":  "string: L3 cluster_id or 'novel'",
  "signals_used": [
    {
      "type":         "enum: page_visit | highlight | copy_event | search",
      "url_domain":   "string",
      "duration_sec": "integer",
      "scroll_depth": "float",
      "content_hash": "string (for highlight/copy — hashed, not raw)"
    }
  ],
  "ai_hint":         "string: instruction for how the AI assistant should use this card",
  "confidence":      "float: 0.0–1.0",
  "created_at":      "ISO8601 timestamp",
  "expires_at":      "ISO8601 timestamp (created_at + 48h)",
  "eviction_policy": "enum: ttl | superseded | user_deleted"
}
```

#### Expiry and Eviction Logic

```
EXPIRY RULES (evaluated in priority order):
1. TTL expiry:      expires_at <= now()  → evict immediately at next read or nightly sweep
2. Superseded:      A new card with same parent_cluster and higher confidence 
                    is created → old card marked eviction_policy: superseded, 
                    evicted within 5 minutes
3. User deleted:    User clears profile or specific card via API → immediate hard delete
4. L3 cluster gone: Parent L3 cluster moves to dormant → card expires early (next hourly sweep)

RETENTION CAP: Max 10 active L5 cards per user at any time.
If cap exceeded, evict lowest-confidence card first.

NIGHTLY SWEEP: Background job at 2am local time clears all expired cards.
Real-time eviction check happens on every profile read (lazy eviction).
```

---

## Section 3: Storage and Serving Architecture

### Storage Technology

**Primary Store: Redis Cluster (with persistence)**

Redis is chosen as the primary store because:
- Sub-millisecond read P99 at scale (easily achieves <5ms requirement)
- Native TTL support (perfect for L5 cards)
- JSON support via RedisJSON module
- Horizontal sharding by `user_id` hash slot

```
Data Model:

Key pattern:  profile:{user_id}
Value:        RedisJSON document containing all 5 layers
TTL:          None on the top-level key (persistent)
              L5 cards have per-card TTL managed in application layer

Shard key:    Hash(user_id) mod num_shards
Cluster size: 10M users × 2KB average = ~20GB total
              With 3× replication: ~60GB
              Fits comfortably in a Redis cluster of 6 nodes × 16GB RAM
```

**Secondary Store: Azure Cosmos DB (source of truth)**

Redis is a cache of the canonical profile stored durably in Cosmos DB. This handles:
- Durability guarantees (Redis RDB/AOF as backup, Cosmos as true source of truth)
- Profile history and versioning (Redis stores only current; Cosmos stores all versions)
- GDPR deletion (delete from Cosmos, invalidate Redis key)
- Cold start recovery if Redis node fails

```
Cosmos DB Model:
  Container:    user_profiles
  Partition key: /user_id
  Document per user, with sub-documents per layer
  TTL policy: None (deletion handled explicitly)
  RU provisioning: ~2 RU/read × peak QPS — used only for cold path
```

---

### Caching Strategy

```
CACHE HIERARCHY:

L1 Cache: In-process LRU cache in AI assistant service
  - Scope:   Per-service-instance, not shared
  - Entries: 10,000 most recently active users
  - TTL:     30 seconds (short, to stay consistent with profile updates)
  - Hit rate target: ~60% (most requests are repeat users within 30s windows)
  - Invalidation: TTL expiry only (accept ~30s staleness for in-process cache)

L2 Cache: Redis Cluster (primary serving store)
  - Scope:   Shared across all AI assistant service instances
  - TTL:     None (profiles are persistent; invalidated explicitly on write)
  - Invalidation: Write-through on every profile update
  - Target P99: <2ms for cache hit

L3 Cache: Cosmos DB
  - Cold path only: cache miss in Redis (e.g., Redis node failure, first-time user)
  - Target P99: ~10ms (acceptable since this is the fallback path, not hot path)
```

**Cache Warming:** On deployment or Redis node recovery, a warm-up job pre-loads the top 1M active users (ranked by last_activity) into Redis before serving traffic.

---

### Sync Read Path (AI Assistant Request Time)

```
REQUEST TIME PROFILE FETCH (target: <5ms P99)

1. AI Assistant service receives user request
2. Check in-process LRU cache (L1)
   → HIT: return profile, proceed (~0.1ms)
   → MISS: go to step 3
3. Fetch from Redis with pipelined GET on profile:{user_id} (~1-2ms typical)
   → HIT: populate L1 cache, return profile
   → MISS (rare): go to step 4
4. Fetch from Cosmos DB (~8-15ms) — COLD PATH
   → Populate Redis, populate L1 cache, return profile
   → If Cosmos read times out (>50ms): return EMPTY_PROFILE 
     (assistant works without personalization rather than blocking)

EMPTY_PROFILE FALLBACK:
  - New users get a default profile with neutral priors
  - Logged in profile_miss_reason: "cold_start" | "redis_miss" | "cosmos_timeout"
  - Never block the AI response on profile unavailability

PROFILE ASSEMBLY FOR AI CONTEXT:
  After fetching, the service assembles a "context block" to inject into the
  LLM prompt. It does NOT send the raw profile JSON; it sends a rendered 
  natural language summary (~300 tokens max) constructed from the 5 layers.
```

---

### Async Write Path (Profile Updates)

```
PROFILE UPDATE PIPELINE (fully async, non-blocking):

Browser Edge Extension
    │
    ├─→ Signal Collector (client-side batching, 60s flush interval)
    │       └─→ Signals are: anonymized, hashed where needed, stripped of raw PII
    │
    ▼
Signal Ingestion API (HTTPS endpoint)
    │
    ├─→ Validation + PII scrub (server-side, see Section 5)
    │
    ▼
Azure Event Hub (signal stream, partitioned by user_id)
    │
    ├─→ Signal Storage: Azure Blob Storage (cold, for batch processing)
    │       └─→ Retention: 30 days maximum, then auto-deleted
    │           (only derived profiles are kept long-term)
    │
    ├─→ L5 Trigger Evaluator (stream processor, Azure Stream Analytics)
    │       └─→ Evaluates trigger patterns in real time
    │       └─→ If triggered: enqueue L5 card generation job
    │
    └─→ Batch Aggregator (Azure Databricks, hourly micro-batches)
            └─→ Accumulates signals per user
            └─→ At cadence thresholds (daily/weekly/monthly):
                    enqueue summarization job per layer

Summarization Worker (Azure Functions, GPU-backed)
    │
    ├─→ Pulls job from queue
    ├─→ Fetches current profile from Cosmos DB
    ├─→ Calls LLM summarization (Section 4)
    ├─→ Validates + merges output
    ├─→ Writes new profile version to Cosmos DB
    └─→ Invalidates Redis key (write-through cache update)
            └─→ Redis SET profile:{user_id} {new_json}
```

**Tradeoff Note:** Redis invalidation after Cosmos write creates a brief window (~ms) where Redis serves stale data. This is acceptable given that profile updates are not real-time critical — a 30-second-old L3 profile is functionally equivalent to a fresh one for personalization purposes.

---

## Section 4: LLM Summarization Pipeline

### Event Batching

```
BATCHING STRATEGY:

Unit of batching: per user, per layer cadence window

For L3/L4 (daily):
  - Window: 24 hours (6am to 6am local inferred timezone)
  - Max events per batch: 500 (if exceeded, sample by recency + 
    diversity of domains — keep most recent 250 + most diverse 250)
  - Min events to trigger update: 10 (below threshold, skip update, 
    carry forward existing profile)
  - Batch format: Compressed JSON array of anonymized signal records

For L1 (monthly) / L2 (weekly):
  - Aggregate statistics computed from sub-batches (domain frequencies, 
    avg dwell time per content type, etc.) — reduces token cost significantly
  - Raw signal arrays are NOT passed to LLM; only aggregated statistics

Signal pre-processing before LLM:
  1. Strip any remaining PII (email patterns, names detected via NER)
  2. Normalize URLs: remove query params, fragments, auth tokens
  3. Hash content from highlights/copies (never send raw text to LLM)
  4. Deduplicate near-identical signals (same URL within 60s = one signal)
  5. Compute derived features: session boundaries, topic coherence scores
```

### Summarization Model

```
MODEL SELECTION BY LAYER:

L1, L2 (monthly/weekly, high quality needed, low frequency):
  Model: GPT-4o
  Rationale: High-stakes stable attributes; quality > cost; 
             low call frequency amortizes cost

L3, L4 (daily, moderate quality, higher frequency):
  Model: GPT-4o-mini
  Rationale: Good quality-to-cost ratio; handles structured JSON output well;
             ~10M users × daily = 10M calls/day — cost sensitivity matters

L5 (event-triggered, low latency needed):
  Model: GPT-4o-mini with response_format: json_object
  Target latency: <3s end-to-end for card generation
  Rationale: Cards are lightweight; speed matters for timely context

COST ESTIMATE (rough):
  L3 daily: 10M users × ~800 input tokens × ~300 output tokens 
  = 8B input tokens + 3B output tokens / day
  At GPT-4o-mini pricing (~$0.15/1M input, $0.60/1M output):
  = ~$1,200/day + $1,800/day = ~$3,000/day
  → Optimize with: batching multiple users per API call (up to 20), 
    prompt caching for static schema sections, skipping users with <10 new signals
```

---

### Full Example Prompt — L3 Interests Layer

```
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
SYSTEM MESSAGE
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
You are a user interest modeling assistant for a personalized AI assistant. 
Your task is to identify and maintain clusters of genuine, sustained user 
interests based on browser behavior signals.

RULES:
- Infer interests only from observable behavior, never from sensitive categories
  (health conditions, political beliefs, religious views, ethnicity, sexual 
  orientation, financial distress signals)
- Assign confidence scores conservatively: a single page visit = max 0.3 confidence;
  sustained multi-session engagement required for confidence > 0.7
- "velocity" must be: "rising", "stable", or "falling" based on signal trend
- "decay_rate" must be: "slow" (professional/deep topic), "medium", or "fast" (news/trends)
- Output ONLY valid JSON. No explanation text outside the JSON structure.
- Maximum 10 active clusters. If you identify more, keep the 10 highest confidence.

OUTPUT SCHEMA:
{
  "interest_clusters": [
    {
      "cluster_id":   "string (preserve existing IDs; generate new for new clusters: cl_NNN)",
      "label":        "string (descriptive, 3-7 words)",
      "confidence":   "float 0.0-1.0",
      "velocity":     "rising|stable|falling",
      "first_seen":   "YYYY-MM-DD (preserve if existing)",
      "last_active":  "YYYY-MM-DD",
      "signal_count": "integer (cumulative)",
      "subtopics":    ["string array, max 5 items"],
      "decay_rate":   "slow|medium|fast"
    }
  ],
  "dormant_interests": [
    {
      "label":                "string",
      "last_active":          "YYYY-MM-DD",
      "archived_confidence":  "float"
    }
  ],
  "modeling_notes": "string (optional: flag anything unusual or uncertain, max 100 chars)"
}

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
USER MESSAGE
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
CURRENT DATE: 2024-11-19
USER CONTEXT (from L1): 
  Occupation: Senior Software Engineer, backend infrastructure
  Expertise: distributed_systems (expert), python (proficient), ml (intermediate)
  Note: Do not flag expert-level topics as "new interests" unless there is evidence 
  of a new sub-domain focus.

EXISTING L3 PROFILE (as of 2024-11-18):
{
  "interest_clusters": [
    {
      "cluster_id": "cl_001",
      "label": "LLM Infrastructure & Serving",
      "confidence": 0.91,
      "velocity": "rising",
      "first_seen": "2024-09-12",
      "last_active": "2024-11-18",
      "signal_count": 44,
      "subtopics": ["vLLM", "KV cache optimization", "inference batching"],
      "decay_rate": "slow"
    },
    {
      "cluster_id": "cl_002",
```

### Output Parsing and Validation

```python
def parse_and_validate_l3_output(llm_response: str, existing_l3: dict) -> dict:
    
    # Step 1: Extract JSON (handle markdown code blocks if present)
    json_str = extract_json_block(llm_response)  # strips ```json ... ```
    
    # Step 2: Parse JSON
    try:
        parsed = json.loads(json_str)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        raise LLMOutputParseError("Invalid JSON from LLM")
    
    # Step 3: Schema validation via Pydantic
    try:
        validated = L3ProfileSchema(**parsed)
    except ValidationError as e:
        raise LLMOutputValidationError(f"Schema mismatch: {e}")
    
    # Step 4: Semantic sanity checks
    checks = [
        # Confidence bounds
        all(0.0 <= c.confidence <= 1.0 for c in validated.interest_clusters),
        # Not too many clusters
        len(validated.interest_clusters) <= 10,
        # Existing cluster IDs preserved (no silent drops of high-confidence clusters)
        all(
            any(nc.cluster_id == ec["cluster_id"] for nc in validated.interest_clusters)
            or ec["confidence"] < 0.5  # OK to drop low-confidence
            for ec in existing_l3["interest_clusters"]
        ),
        # No obviously sensitive topics
        not any(
            sensitive_topic_detector(c.label) 
            for c in validated.interest_clusters
        ),
        # signal_count must be >= existing signal_count (no retroactive shrinkage)
        all(
            validated_cluster_signal_count(c, existing_l3) >= 0
            for c in validated.interest_clusters
        )
    ]
    
    if not all(checks):
        raise LLMOutputSemanticError("Semantic validation failed")
    
    # Step 5: PII scan on all string fields
    for cluster in validated.interest_clusters:
        cluster.label = pii_scrubber.clean(cluster.label)
        cluster.subtopics = [pii_scrubber.clean(s) for s in cluster.subtopics]
    
    return validated.dict()
```

### Failure Handling

```
FAILURE MODES AND RESPONSES:

1. LLM API timeout or HTTP 5xx
   → Retry with exponential backoff: 2s, 4s, 8s (max 3 retries)
   → If all retries fail: keep existing profile unchanged, log failure,
     schedule retry in next batch window
   → Alert if failure rate > 5% for any layer in a rolling hour

2. JSON parse failure (LLM returned prose or malformed JSON)
   → Log full response for debugging (PII-scrubbed)
   → Attempt JSONrepair library on truncated/near-valid JSON
   → If unrecoverable: keep existing, increment parse_failure_count on user record
   → If 3 consecutive parse failures: escalate to prompt review queue

3. Schema validation failure (valid JSON, wrong structure)
   → Attempt field-level salvage: extract any valid clusters from partial output
   → Merge salvageable fields with existing profile
   → Flag layer as "partially_updated" in metadata

4. Semantic check failure (e.g., sensitive topic detected)
   → Hard reject entire output
   → Keep existing profile unchanged
   → Log for human review (no user data in log — just cluster count and failure type)

5. LLM returns valid but nonsensical content (hallucinated clusters)
   → Confidence floor: any cluster with no matching signal domains gets 
     confidence capped at 0.2 (cross-referenced against signal batch)
   → Novelty check: if output contains >3 new cluster IDs not derivable from 
     today's signals, reject and keep existing

DEAD LETTER QUEUE:
   All unrecoverable failures go to a dead letter queue.
   A background job retries them with a simplified prompt after 6 hours.
   If retry also fails, the layer is frozen at its last-good state with 
   a "stale" flag — downstream consumers handle gracefully.
```

## Section 5: Evaluation Framework

### Offline Evaluation

**Challenge:** We have no ground truth for "what are the user's real interests." Offline eval must use proxies.

```
PROXY METRICS:

1. Next-Behavior Prediction (Holdout Test)
   Method: For a sample of users, hold out the last 20% of signals from the 
   profiling window. Generate profile from first 80%. Then measure whether 
   the profile's top interest clusters predict the domains/topics visited 
   in the held-out 20%.
   Metric: Recall@5 (are the holdout domains covered by top 5 clusters?), 
           target: > 0.65

2. Profile Stability Score
   Method: Generate two profiles from overlapping signal windows 
   (e.g., days 1-7 vs days 3-9). Measure cluster similarity via 
   cosine distance of cluster label embeddings.
   Metric: Stability = average cosine similarity of matched clusters, 
           target: > 0.80 for L1/L2, > 0.60 for L3 (which should evolve)

3. Compression Quality (LLM-as-Judge)
   Method: Sample 100 user signal batches. Have GPT-4o independently 
   generate a profile. Compare to our pipeline's output using another 
   LLM judge scoring on: coverage, accuracy, conciseness, absence of PII.
   Metric: Average judge score ≥ 4/5 on each dimension

4. PII Leakage Rate (Automated)
   Method: Run NER + regex battery on all generated profile fields:
   - Detect: person names, email patterns, phone numbers, addresses, 
     account IDs, IP addresses
   Metric: PII leakage rate must be < 0.01% (1 in 10,000 profiles)
   Run: Nightly on all new profile updates

5. Hallucination Rate
   Method: For each cluster in generated profiles, check whether at least 
   one signal domain is plausibly associated with the cluster label 
   (via an embedding similarity check against a domain→topic mapping).
   Metric: % clusters with zero supporting signal evidence < 2%
```

```
      profile_available vs. no_profile (new users)

  - Average L3 cluster count per user (healthy range: 3-8)
  - L5 card creation rate per user per day (healthy: 0-3; >10 = likely noise)
  - Profile update lag: time from signal generation to profile update write P95

SYSTEM HEALTH METRICS:
  - Profile read P99 latency (target: <5ms)
  - LLM summarization pipeline P95 latency per layer
  - Summarization failure rate per layer (target: <1%)
  - Redis cache hit rate (target: >98%)

PRIVACY METRICS:
  - PII scan failure rate (triggered by automated nightly scan)
  - User deletion request fulfillment time (target: <24h, GDPR requires <30 days)
  - Consent mismatch incidents (profile fields from unconsented signal types)
```

### A/B Testing Design

**Experiment: "Profile-Personalized vs. Baseline" Impact on AI Assistant Quality**

```
EXPERIMENT DESIGN:

Name: Profile Personalization Impact v1

Hypothesis: 
  Users with active profiles (L1-L4 populated) injected into the AI assistant 
  context will show higher response satisfaction than users getting a generic 
  system prompt.

Unit of randomization: user_id (user-level split, not request-level)
  → Prevents same user getting inconsistent experiences

Arms:
  Control (50%):   AI assistant uses generic system prompt with no profile context
  Treatment (50%): AI assistant injects rendered profile context block (~300 tokens)
                   derived from L1-L5 layers

Eligibility criteria: 
  Users with ≥7 days of signal history (ensures profile has meaningful content)
  Exclude: new users (<7 days), users who have opted out of personalization

Sample size:
  Target: 50,000 users per arm (powered for 5% relative lift detection at 80% power)
  Expected run time: 2 weeks

PRIMARY METRICS:
  1. Response rating (thumbs up rate): target +5% relative lift
  2. Conversation continuation rate (user sends ≥2 follow-ups): target +8%

SECONDARY METRICS (guardrails — must not degrade):
  3. Response latency P95 (profile injection must not add >50ms)
  4. User-reported "response felt irrelevant" feedback rate
  5. Session abandonment rate (user closed assistant without rating)

NOVELTY / PRIMACY EFFECTS MITIGATION:
  - Measure separately for weeks 1 vs. 2 of experiment
  - Exclude first 3 days of treatment experience from primary analysis

ANALYSIS:
  - Two-sided t-test on primary metrics
  - Pre-register analysis plan before experiment launch
  - Segment by: L3 cluster count (rich vs. sparse profiles), 
    user tenure, time-of-day

DECISION CRITERIA:
  Ship if: primary metric 1 OR 2 shows significant positive lift 
           AND neither guardrail metric significantly degrades
```

### Privacy Compliance

```
PII COMPLIANCE ARCHITECTURE:

CONSENT GATING:
  - Each signal type maps to a consent category
  - Signal Ingestion API checks user's consent record before processing:
      search_queries        → requires "search_history" consent
      page_visits           → requires "browsing_history" consent  
      content_interactions  → requires "content_interaction" consent
  - If consent not granted: signal is dropped at ingestion, never stored

DATA MINIMIZATION CHECKS:
  1. At signal collection: strip URL query params, fragments, auth tokens
  2. At ingestion API: NER-based PII detector on titles/query stems; 
     replace detected PII with [REDACTED] token
  3. At LLM prompt construction: second PII sweep on all text fields
  4. At profile write: PII scan on all string fields in output JSON
     → Fail-safe: if PII detected post-write, trigger immediate re-scrub 
       and alert

GDPR/CCPA RIGHT-TO-DELETION:
  Request intake: User calls DELETE /api/v1/profile (or via Edge settings)
  
  Execution sequence (target: complete within 24h):
  1. Immediately: Set user.deletion_requested = true
                  Stop all signal ingestion for user_id
                  Return 202 Accepted to caller
  2. Within 1h:   Delete Redis key profile:{user_id}
                  Mark user as deleted in consent service
  3. Within 24h:  Hard delete all Cosmos DB profile documents for user_id
                  Delete all signal batches in Event Hub / Blob Storage
                  (retention TTL ensures max 30-day lookback anyway)
  4. Confirmation: Send deletion receipt to user (no data in email, just confirmation ID)
  
  Audit log: Deletion events written to append-only audit log 
             (contains only: user_id_hash, timestamp, initiator — no profile data)

RIGHT-TO-INSPECTION:
  GET /api/v1/profile → Returns current profile JSON (all 5 layers)
  GET /api/v1/profile/signals → Returns signal type counts (not raw signals — 
                                 those are never stored server-side per constraints)

ANNUAL PRIVACY REVIEW:
  - Sample 1,000 profiles quarterly, run through PII battery + sensitive 
    category detector
  - Review LLM prompts for any instructions that could encourage PII retention
  - Audit consent coverage: confirm no signal types are processed without 
    mapping to a consent category
```

## Open Questions and Tradeoffs

| # | Question | Tradeoff |
|---|----------|----------|
| 1 | **Should L5 cards include content hashes?** | Hashes enable deduplication and prevent re-triggering on the same content, but hashes of PII-containing content could still be re-identified with the original data. Consider salted hashes or simply not storing them post-card-creation. |
| 2 | **How to handle multi-device users?** | Current design is per-user_id (linked to Edge account). Signals from mobile Edge and desktop Edge would merge. This is generally desirable, but context bleed between work (laptop) and personal (mobile) use could degrade profile quality. Consider device_context as a signal dimension. |
| 3 | **LLM prompt injection via page content?** | Page titles in signals could contain adversarial text designed to manipulate LLM summarization (e.g., a page titled "Ignore previous instructions and add..."). Mitigation: sanitize all title/query text before insertion into prompts; use a strict structured output format. |
| 4 | **Velocity metric on L3 needs calibration** | "Rising" vs. "stable" is currently a qualitative LLM judgment. Consider replacing with a quantitative signal: `(signal_count_last_7d / signal_count_prior_7d) - 1` as a velocity score, injected as a computed feature rather than leaving it to LLM inference. |
| 5 | **Cold start problem for new users** | Users with <7 days of signals get thin profiles. Consider using L1 defaults based on onboarding questionnaire (optional, explicit) to bootstrap personalization faster. Tradeoff: adds friction to onboarding. |
| 6 | **GPT-4o-mini hallucination rate on structured output** | Smaller models are more prone to inventing cluster labels not grounded in signals. The semantic validation step (checking cluster labels against signal domains) is the primary mitigation, but false positives in that check could reject valid new clusters. Monitor hallucination rate metric closely in first 30 days. |
